description: The smartest engineers in the observable universe 🪐
summary:
Echoes of Exploration is an interactive website that tells kids the story of the machines NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space.

It starts with a guided “road trip” to six machines: the Apollo 11 lander, the Apollo 15 lunar rover, the Opportunity rover, the Ingenuity helicopter, Cassini and Voyager 1. Kids can watch 3D replays of the landings and walk around a Mars landing site in first person. They can explore an atlas of 79 objects on the Moon, Mars and beyond, fly through the solar system, and read the story behind each mission’s last signal.

The challenge asks how to make this hardware matter to school-age kids. We answer it by letting them explore instead of read. Each machine has a short, kid-friendly story about what it did, how it ended and where it is now. Every image is credited to its source, most of them NASA.

It matters because these machines carry the history of exploration, and many of them are still out there. Some, like Voyager, are still sending signals home. Showing kids that they were “abandoned, but not forgotten” turns old hardware into curiosity about science and about where we go next.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS
Echoes of Exploration is an interactive website that tells school-age kids the story of the machines NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. It has five parts:

  • Tour: a guided “road trip” to six machines: the Apollo 11 lunar module, the Apollo 15 lunar rover, Opportunity, Ingenuity, Cassini and Voyager 1. Each stop replays the machine’s arrival in 3D and tells its story in short chapters.
  • Atlas: 79 objects placed on globes of the Moon, Mars, Earth orbit and deep space, with a timeline of when each one arrived. Kids can also walk around a Mars landing site in first person.
  • Solar system: a 3D map you can search to find where each machine is now.
  • Fly: kids pilot a spacecraft between the planets.
  • Signals: the last messages these machines sent home, including Voyager, which is still sending.
    All content comes from JSON data files, so new missions can be added without changing code.

BENEFITS
Kids learn by exploring instead of reading long text. Every object is real, and every image is credited to its source, mostly NASA. The site runs in an ordinary web browser with nothing to install, so it works in classrooms, and it is easy to extend.

INTENDED IMPACT
We want kids to see this hardware as chapters in a story that is still going, not as space junk. Discovering that a car is parked on the Moon, or that Voyager is still sending signals, can spark a lasting interest in science, engineering and exploration. It also introduces the idea that people leave things behind wherever they explore.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, Python and JSON.
  • Website: Next.js, React and Tailwind CSS.
  • 3D: Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, Motion for animation, Lucide icons, and NASA 3D models compressed with Draco.
  • Our own Python tools: one converts NASA 3D models, and another refuses to include any image without a recorded credit and licence.
  • Trailer: ffmpeg, Playwright, edge-tts text-to-speech, and an original soundtrack generated in Python with NumPy.
  • Sources: NASA images, models and video, plus Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) images from NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University, used with credit for education.
  • Hardware: an ordinary Windows PC.

CREATIVITY
It is a road trip, not an encyclopedia: the machines are the characters, and their story is where they are now. 3D replays let kids watch each landing happen. The signals page tells each mission’s ending through its final transmission, which makes these machines feel personal. Our trailer uses music we composed in code.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Audience: short sentences, big visuals and no jargon.
  • Accuracy: dates, locations and outcomes come from NASA sources.
  • Licensing: every image is public domain, CC BY or CC BY-SA, or LROC with credit, and our tools enforce it.
  • Performance: compressed models keep the site fast on school computers.
  • Scope: six machines explored in depth, plus a broad atlas of 79 objects.
